title: The Effects of Rehabilitation Exercise and Functional Back Training on Strength and Pain Perception in Patients with Chronic Low Back Pain.
summary:
This study investigates whether additional functional back training can reduce pain and improve trunk muscle strength in people with chronic low back pain.
The study includes adults who participate in physician-prescribed orthopaedic rehabilitation exercise because of their back pain. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Both groups attend rehabilitation exercise once per week for 12 weeks. One group also takes part in a 45-minute functional back-training session once per week and completes a short guided home exercise programme of no more than 15 minutes once per week.
Assessments are conducted before the start of the study, after the 12-week training period, and again four weeks later. These assessments include self-reported pain intensity, sensitivity to pressure in the back region, trunk muscle strength, limitations in daily activities, and health-related quality of life.
The aim is to determine whether adding functional back training leads to greater improvements than rehabilitation exercise alone and whether any effects are maintained after the training period has ended.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Physician-prescribed orthopaedic rehabilitation exercise
- Chronic non-specific low back pain
- Pain located above the lumbosacral junction and below the costal margin
- Ability to understand the study information and provide written informed consent independently
Exclusion criteria:
- Inability to provide informed consent
- Diagnosed tumours
- Fractures and/or osteoporosis
- Infectious or rheumatic diseases of the spine
- Acute or serious comorbidities that may compromise safe participation in the exercise programme or study assessments
